Check conditional expectation, invariant range and idempotence in L².

locators.locator: Proposition proof, projection formula (2) and verification, p.2

proofDependencies.title: Local characters form a dense family
proofDependencies.statement: Functions depending on finitely many p-adic coordinates and valuation shells, with characters of local unit quotients, span a dense subspace of L²(Ẑ,μβ).
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Approximate by finite-coordinate cylinder functions.
Decompose each coordinate into its countable valuation shells.
Use finite character orthogonality on the compact local unit quotients.

locators.locator: Proposition proof, local characters and valuation translates, pp.2–3

proofDependencies.title: Reciprocal primes in progressions
proofDependencies.statement: Fix N≥1 and a coprime to N. The fixed-progression prime asymptotic π(X;N,a)∼Li(X)/φ(N) implies Σp≤X,p≡a(modN)1/p=(1/φ(N))log log X+o(log log X). In particular Σp≡a(modN)p^(−β) diverges for 0<β≤1.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Apply partial summation to π(t;N,a): π(X)/X+integral from 2 to X of π(t)/t² dt.
Use the asymptotic with a fixed relative error on large t and squeeze the integral against (1/φ(N)) integral dt/(t log t).

locators.locator: Proposition proof, p.3 (Dirichlet input); partial summation is the local refinement

proofDependencies.title: Nontrivial characters are annihilated in the critical interval
proofDependencies.statement: For0<β≤1 and a nontrivial local unit characterχ, the increasing-prime projections P_Aχ tend to0: their product coefficients contain factors (1−p^(−β))/(1−χ(p)p^(−β)), and divergence of the prime reciprocal sum in a suitable character sector forces the product to0.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Compute the geometric prime-power factors in the finite-prime average.
Choose a congruence sector where Reχ(p)<0.
Use the fixed-progression prime theorem to obtain divergence of Σp p^(−β), not merely infinitude of primes.

locators.locator: Proposition proof, nontrivial character product and progression argument, p.3

proofDependencies.title: Decreasing orthogonal projections
proofDependencies.statement: Let Hn be a decreasing sequence of closed subspaces of a Hilbert space and H=intersection Hn. Their orthogonal projections Pn satisfy ‖Pn v−P v‖→0 for every v. In the finite-prime exhaustion, Hn consists of functions invariant under multiplication by all primes in its first n entries.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: For m≥n, orthogonality gives ‖Pn v−Pm v‖²=‖Pn v‖²−‖Pm v‖².
The decreasing norm squares make Pn v Cauchy. Its limit lies in every Hn and has the defining projection orthogonality to H.

locators.locator: Projection exhaustion in the Proposition proof, p.2

proofDependencies.title: Ergodic scaling measure is extreme
proofDependencies.statement: For 0<β≤1, if μβ=tμ1+(1−t)μ2 for normalized β-scaling measures and 0<t<1, then μ1=μ2=μβ. The Radon–Nikodym density dμ1/dμβ is bounded by 1/t and Q+×-invariant, hence constant by ergodicity; normalization makes the constant one.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Domination by the convex combination bounds the Radon-Nikodym density. Equal scaling laws make the density invariant under every rational dilation. Ergodicity makes it constant; normalization fixes the constant and then both summands.

locators.locator: Corollary proof, p.3; direct measure form of extremality

proofDependencies.title: Unit average of a scaling measure
proofDependencies.statement: For any normalized β-scaling measure μ, its average over W=Ẑ× with normalized Haar measure is again normalized and β-scaling, is W-invariant, and equals the canonical product-density μβ. Equality follows from finite valuation/unit cylinders, then a countable rational-dilate exhaustion of A_f.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: On every compact rational dilate, integrate the finite measures over compact W; Fubini gives normalization and scaling.
W invariance makes unit residues Haar and scaling fixes each valuation-shell mass. Cylinder uniqueness yields the product measure.

locators.locator: Unique W-invariant measure, p.2; Corollary argument, p.3

proofDependencies.title: Extreme unit average is constant
proofDependencies.statement: Let μ be a normalized scaling measure whose compact-unit average is the extreme μβ. Then u_*μ=μβ for every u∈W. For any finite-measure cylinder test, a nonconstant continuous value in u would split Haar into two positive pieces and give a nontrivial convex decomposition of μβ. Cylinder tests separate measures; setting u=1 proves μ=μβ.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Evaluate the unit translates on compact-cylinder test functions. If one value varies continuously, two positive-Haar pieces yield distinct normalized averaged scaling measures whose convex combination is the canonical extreme. This contradiction makes all test integrals constant; separating tests and the identity unit recover the original measure.

locators.locator: Corollary conclusion and averaging argument, p.3

proofDependencies.title: Diagonal expectation in the full corner
proofDependencies.statement: The reduced crossed product has the positive contractive expectation E(Σq fq Uq)=f1. Its compression to pBp maps to C(Ẑ), preserves 1 and is faithful. The dynamics multiplies the q-term by q^(it).
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Import the identity-coefficient expectation of the reduced crossed product from OP2-expectation-measure. Compress by the compact-open integral projection. Positivity, contractivity and faithfulness survive compression, and the compressed unit maps to the constant one function.

locators.locator: Laca §3.2, p.9; Neshveyev 2000 scaling correspondence, p.1

proofDependencies.title: Scaling measure produces a KMS state
proofDependencies.statement: For β>0 and a normalized β-scaling μ, the functional φμ(a)=∫Ẑ E(a) dμ is a completed KMSβ state. The rational covariance and μ(qE)=q^(−β)μ(E) prove the core KMS identity. It is positive and normalized by the expectation.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Integrate the corner expectation against the normalized measure. Check the core KMS identity on two finite crossed-product monomials using the rational scaling law and covariance. Linearity and the dense-core strip equivalence give the completed state.

proofDependencies.title: KMS restriction reconstructs a scaling measure
proofDependencies.statement: For β>0, restrict φ to C(Ẑ) and use the existing positive-functional measure representation. The KMS dilation identity implies ν(nE)=n^(−β)ν(E). This extends uniquely to a Radon μ on A_f with μ(Ẑ)=1 and μ(qE)=q^(−β)μ(E). Nonidentity rational terms have zero expectation in φ: use dynamics invariance when q≠1.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Represent the diagonal restriction by the imported positive-functional measure theorem. The KMS identity for dilations gives scaling on integral compact opens, and exhaustion extends it uniquely to finite adeles. Dynamics invariance kills all terms with rational index different from 1; diagonal uniqueness proves reconstruction.

proofDependencies.title: Unit-orbit decomposition above the critical temperature
proofDependencies.statement: Forβ>1, the disjoint sets nẐ× cover a μβ-full subset ofẐ, and μβ(Ẑ×)=∏p(1−p^(−β))=ζ(β)^(−1). Every scaling measure is reconstructed from a probability measure onẐ× by the weighted orbit sums.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Use the convergent Euler product for the unit mass.
Apply the scaling law to disjoint n-unit orbits.
The weighted masses sum to1, proving full measure and the reconstruction.

proofDependencies.title: High-beta unit-mass reconstruction
proofDependencies.statement: For β>1 any normalized scaling μ is carried by the disjoint sets qW, q∈Q_+×, W=Ẑ×, and μ(W)=1/ζ(β). Its normalized unit restriction ν=ζ(β) μ|W is a probability measure. Conversely μν=ζ(β)⁻¹Σq∈Q_+× q^(−β)(q_*ν) is the unique scaling measure with that unit restriction.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: For the normalization on Ẑ, only q∈N+ contributes, giving ζ(β).
On compact rational dilates the sum is finite as a measure after the same convergent bound.
Recover each qW component by scaling; the complement is null by the high-beta orbit theorem.

proofDependencies.title: Probability measures parameterize high-beta KMS states
proofDependencies.statement: For β>1, ν↦∫W φβ,u dν(u) is an affine homeomorphism from Radon probability measures on the existing compact group W=Ẑ× to completed KMSβ states. The inverse is the normalized unit restriction of the corresponding scaling measure.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Restrict the scaling measure to units and multiply by zeta(beta). The rational-orbit decomposition reconstructs it and yields the Gibbs barycentre. Integrals against continuous test functions give weak continuity of both maps; the state topology is pointwise weak evaluation.

proofDependencies.title: High-beta extreme states
proofDependencies.statement: For β>1 the extreme KMS states are precisely φβ,u, u∈W; equality of two such states forces equality of their unit parameters. Dirac probability measures are exactly the extremes of ProbabilityMeasure W under the preceding affine homeomorphism.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Transport extreme points through the affine probability-measure correspondence. Probability measures on a compact Hausdorff space are extreme exactly when Dirac; injectivity of the correspondence separates unit parameters.

proofDependencies.title: Profinite units act on rational torsion
proofDependencies.statement: The imported Ẑ× maps to AddAut(Q/Z) by its compatible residues u_N acting on each N-torsion subgroup. This is bijective and continuous in the topology of finite restrictions; every torsion element belongs to one of these finite subgroups.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Restrict an additive automorphism to every cyclic N-torsion subgroup and identify it with an invertible residue modulo N. These residues are compatible under divisibility, yielding a profinite unit. Conversely compatible residues act consistently on the union of all torsion subgroups; finite evaluations prove continuity.

proofDependencies.title: Symmetry on the high-beta extreme boundary
proofDependencies.statement: For β>1, pullback by θ_v maps φβ,u to φβ,uv, with composition conventions fixed by the action on Q/Z. Therefore W acts freely and transitively on the high-beta extreme boundary.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Apply the symmetry to each torsion generator in the Gibbs formula. The resulting character is the product of the two unit parameters. The injective identification of extremes with units then gives freeness and transitivity.

proofDependencies.title: Finite cotangent Fourier identity
proofDependencies.statement: For N>0 and ζ^N=1, Σ1≤j<N(j/N−1/2)ζ^j equals (ζ+1)/(2(ζ−1)) when ζ≠1 and equals 0 when ζ=1. The nontrivial value is cot(πt)/(2i) for ζ=exp(2πit). Passing to a multiple of N gives the same value for every N-torsion character; finite Fourier injectivity proves level independence in Q[Q/Z].
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Differentiate the finite geometric sum and evaluate at a nontrivial Nth root.
At ζ=1 sum the rational coefficients directly; their sum is zero.
Evaluate both levels at all characters of their common finite cyclic group and use finite Fourier injectivity.

locators.locator: Ch.3, Lemma 3.28 and its finite Abel-summation proof, pp.464–465

proofDependencies.title: Möbius divisibility identities
proofDependencies.statement: For fn(j)=Σd|j μ(d)(j/d)^n, the projection sum Σd|N fn(d)πd evaluates on a Q-lattice to m^n, where m is the order of its N-torsion kernel. Keep n=1 and n=1−k, including negative exponents.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Write divisibility projections as indicator functions of divisors of m.
Use finite Möbius inversion.
Retain rational negative powers when deriving the k-division relation.

proofDependencies.title: The Eisenstein division formula
proofDependencies.statement: For k≥1, ΣNa=0 ek,a=γk Σd|N[(2^k−2)f1(d)+N^k f1−k(d)]πd, with γk=(2πi)^(−k)Σy∈Z\{0} y^(−k) in the source normalization (symmetric principal value for k=1; absolute convergence for k>1). For odd k the vanishing is interpreted consistently. Both the arithmetic coefficients and the degenerate-value convention are fixed by the preceding identities.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Count the m-fold fibres of the N-torsion map.
Evaluate the nondegenerate trigonometric sum plus the degenerate correction.
Replace powers of m by the Möbius projection sums.

proofDependencies.title: Recovering prime-power divisibility projections
proofDependencies.statement: All projections πp^b belong to the Q-algebra generated by e1,a. For odd p, solve the k=2 division relation inductively in b. For p=2 the leading π2^b coefficient vanishes, so use the relation at N=2^(b+1) to recover π2^b; e.g. π2=3+2Σ4a=0 e2,a.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Compute the leading coefficient−p^(b−1)(2−3p+p²).
For p=2 retain the nonzero next projection coefficient at the doubled torsion level.
Use coprime products to recover allπN.

locators.locator: Chapter 3, proof of Theorem 3.30, prime-power and doubled dyadic level step, pp.467–468

proofDependencies.title: Rational power sums in a prime corner
proofDependencies.statement: Let N=p^b, e=1−πp, and zj=e e1,j/N for 1≤j<N in the unital corner eQ[Q/Z]. The division formula gives Σj Pk(zj)=(N^k−1)γk e for every k≥1, where Pk is evaluated with corner unit e. Since Pk is monic of degree k, triangular induction gives Σj zj^k∈Qe. Zero roots and repeated roots are retained; there are N−1 indices.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Multiply the division identity by e and subtract the j=0 term Pk(0)e.
Solve successively for each ordinary power sum using the monic polynomial Pk and previously known lower powers.

proofDependencies.title: Newton identities in the reduced corner
proofDependencies.statement: For the N−1 commuting elements zj in the preceding corner, all elementary symmetric functions σh(z1,…,zN−1) belong to Qe. Hence QN(X)=∏j=1..N−1(X−zj) is a monic degree-N−1 polynomial with rational scalar coefficients in that corner and QN(z1)=0.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Use hσh=Σk=1..h(−1)^(k−1)σh−k sk over Q.
Division by each positive h is permitted, so induction gives rational coefficients.
The product polynomial vanishes at z1 by its first factor; its degree is N−1 regardless of zero-root multiplicity.

proofDependencies.title: Roots of the reduced polynomial
proofDependencies.statement: At an invertible Q-lattice, QN has multiset of roots cot(πj/N)/(2i), 1≤j<N. A unit character permutes this multiset. These roots are purely imaginary, so 1/2 is never a root. For even N the root at j=N/2 is zero and must be retained.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Evaluate the corner polynomial in an invertible lattice and list all N-1 nontrivial torsion characters. A unit permutes this list. Each cotangent is real, so its division by 2i is purely imaginary and differs from 1/2; the even-level zero remains a root.

proofDependencies.title: Polynomial recovery of the Cayley transform
proofDependencies.statement: Since QN(1/2)≠0, gcd(QN,2X−1)=1 in Q[X]. Bézout yields U,V∈Q[X] with U(2X−1)+VQN=1. In the reduced corner, 2z1−e is invertible with inverse U(z1), and (2z1+e)U(z1)=e e(1/N). Thus this root-of-unity component lies in the Eisenstein algebra.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Evaluate the Bézout identity at z1; QN(z1)=0.
Use the finite cotangent Fourier identity to identify (2z1+e)/(2z1−e) with e times the root of unity.

proofDependencies.title: Eisenstein algebra is stable under semigroup endomorphisms
proofDependencies.statement: For αn(f)=μn f μn*, αn(ek,a)=πn ek,a/n, independently of the chosen n-preimage a/n. The projections πn belong to the algebra generated by first functions, so αn preserves that algebra.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Apply dilation covariance to every term of the finite first-function Fourier expression. It produces the range projection times the selected preimage expression; different preimages agree after multiplying by that projection. Polynomial evaluation gives all higher functions.

locators.locator: Ch.3, (3.98)–(3.99), pp.464–465; final induction in Theorem 3.30, pp.469–470

proofDependencies.title: Reassembly of the prime-power components
proofDependencies.statement: For N=p^b, the (1−πp)e(1/N) component is supplied by the Cayley lemma. The other component is πp e(1/N)=αp(e(p/N)); the induction hypothesis at p^(b−1) and semigroup preservation put it in the Eisenstein algebra. At b=1 its lower-level input is e(0)=1. Adding the complementary components recovers e(1/N).
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Split e(1/N) by the complementary prime projection. The Cayley lemma recovers the complementary corner; semigroup covariance expresses the prime-projection part through the lower-level torsion element. Induct on b with e(0)=1 as the base.

locators.locator: Ch.3, last part of Theorem 3.30 proof, pp.469–470

proofDependencies.title: Recovering roots of unity from Eisenstein functions
proofDependencies.statement: Every e(a), a∈Q/Z, belongs to the Q-algebra generated by first trigonometric Eisenstein functions. Prime-power denominators follow from reduced-corner Newton identities, the Bézout Cayley inverse and the explicit lower-level induction. General denominators follow by writing a as a sum of its prime-primary components and using e(a+b)=e(a)e(b).
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Apply the prime-level induction separately to each prime power in the denominator.
Decompose the torsion point into prime-primary summands and multiply the recovered roots.

proofDependencies.title: Compatible finite cyclotomic restrictions
proofDependencies.statement: For every field automorphism τ of C fixing Q, the exponents v_N∈(Z/NZ)× defined by τ(ζ_N)=ζ_N^(v_N) are compatible under divisibility. Conversely compatible exponents define an automorphism of Qcycl. The imported finite cyclotomic Galois identifications supply each v_N; the transition verification supplies their inverse-limit element v∈Ẑ×.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Import each finite cyclotomic Galois identification. Restriction to smaller cyclotomic fields equates the exponents modulo their levels. The compatible family acts on the union Qcycl and yields the profinite unit; no global Artin theorem is needed.

proofDependencies.title: Mod-eight character matrix orthogonality
proofDependencies.statement: For H_i,a=ψi(2a+1), i,a∈{0,1,2,3}, H Hᵀ=HᵀH=4I. Thus Hᵀ/4 gives the exact inverse between twist coordinates and residue coordinates.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Write the four character rows on the four odd residues. Distinct rows have dot product zero and each squared norm is four. The same calculation on columns proves the inverse matrix formula.

locators.locator: Proof of Lemma 2, character projections in (31)–(35), pp.362–363

proofDependencies.title: Normal convergence in the first tube
proofDependencies.statement: On each compact K⊂{Res>1,Rew>1}, the odd (n,d) summands have a summable majorant n^(−σ0)d^(−ν0) with σ0,ν0>1. Consequently their double sum is normally convergent on K.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Take the minima of the two real parts on the compact set; both exceed one. Bound every character by one and dominate the double sum by the product of two convergent positive Dirichlet series. The bound is independent of the point in the compact set.

proofDependencies.title: Absolute convergence in the initial double tube
proofDependencies.statement: For Res>1 and Rew>1 the odd n,d double sum is absolutely convergent, locally uniformly on compact sub-tubes; hence it may be summed in either order.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Bound both characters by1.
Dominate by ζ(Res)ζ(Rew); the correcting ζ2 factor has Re(2s+2w−1)>1.
Use compact positive margins for locally uniform domination.

locators.locator: §3 proof of Lemma 2, initial expansion (28), pp.361–362

proofDependencies.title: Unique odd squarefree factorization
proofDependencies.statement: Every positive odd d is uniquely d0k² with d0 positive odd squarefree and k positive odd. The Jacobi symbol χd equals χd0 away from prime divisors of k and vanishes at those prime divisors.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Split each prime exponent into its parity and an even part. Unique factorization gives the squarefree component and square component, retaining oddness. The Jacobi factors for even exponents are one away from their prime and zero at it.

proofDependencies.title: Quadratic conductor and root number
proofDependencies.statement: For each odd squarefree d0 and twist i identify χd0ψi with its primitive real character of conductor q_i,η d0, parity κ_i and root number +1. Removed prime-2 and square-factor Euler factors agree with L2. Here η=d0 mod8, q and κ are exactly the table defining the reflection block; principal cases use meromorphic germs.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Identify the signed fundamental-discriminant character with the pinned primitive character. Prove the conductor, parity and positive Gauss-sum root number, then apply the pinned completed functional equation and change-level formula. These arithmetic/Gauss-sum adapters remain the named source gap.

proofDependencies.title: Nonzero squarefree-series denominator
proofDependencies.statement: For Re(s+2w)>1 the Euler product of L2(s+2w,χd0ψi) is nonzero. On any closed sub-half-plane Re(s+2w)≥1+δ, its reciprocal is bounded by ζ(1+δ), uniformly in d0 and the twist.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Use the absolutely convergent Euler product on the strict right half-plane. Each reciprocal local factor has modulus at most 1+p^(-sigma), whose product is at most zeta(sigma). This proves nonvanishing and the compact sub-half-plane uniform bound.

proofDependencies.title: Separating square factors of the discriminant index
proofDependencies.statement: Each odd d has a unique d=d0 d1² with d0 squarefree. In the initial tube, Z=ζ2(2s+2w−1)ζ2(2w)Σd0 odd squarefree L2(s,χd0ψ)ψ′(d0)/(d0^w L2(s+2w,χd0ψ)).
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Factor d uniquely prime by prime.
Removing primes dividing d1 from the inner L-series gives the finite missing Euler factors.
Sum each geometric square-factor series absolutely to obtain the quotient in (29).

proofDependencies.title: Quadratic fourth moment
proofDependencies.statement: For fixed σ∈[1/2,1] and ε>0, Σχ nonprincipal primitive real,condχ≤Q |L(σ+it,χ)|⁴ ≤ Cσ,ε [Q+(Q(1+|t|))^(2−2σ)](Q(1+|t|))^ε, for Q≥1 and t∈R. The conductor-one principal character is treated separately.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Use the quadratic large sieve on the smoothed Dirichlet polynomial for L².
Bound the reflected contour using the primitive functional equation; bootstrap the dyadic fourth moment and treat σ=1/2 by σ=1/2−ε.

proofDependencies.title: Primitive quadratic first moment
proofDependencies.statement: On σ=1/2, Hölder and the O(X) count of primitive real characters of conductor≤8X give Σd0≤X,d0 odd squarefree,χd0ψi nonprincipal |L(1/2+it,χd0ψi)| ≤ Cε X^(1+ε)(1+|t|)^(1/4+ε).
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Apply Holder with fourth power to the primitive family. The character count contributes X^(3/4), and the fourth-moment bound contributes X^(1/4+epsilon)(1+|t|)^(1/4+epsilon), after rescaling epsilon. Remove principal terms before applying the supplied moment.

proofDependencies.title: Imprimitive square-factor bound
proofDependencies.statement: For d=d0k² odd, the deleted Euler factors give |L2(s,χdψi)| ≤ |L2(s,χd0ψi)|∏p|k(1+p^(−Res)). On a fixed real strip with Res≥1/2 this product is Oε(k^ε), uniformly in Ims. Summing k≤√(X/d0) transports the primitive first moment to all odd d; the d0=1 principal term uses ζ2(s), off s=1.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Use the change-level identity to write the omitted prime factors. Bound them by the product of 1+p^(-sigma), absorb that product in k^epsilon on the fixed strip, and sum the primitive estimate over square factors. Treat the sole principal primitive term by the meromorphic odd zeta function.

proofDependencies.title: The first-moment input for the wider convergence tube
proofDependencies.statement: For every ε>0 and twist i there is Cε>0 such that, for all X≥1 and t∈R, Σ1≤d≤X,d odd |L2(1/2+it,χdψi)| ≤ Cε X^(1+ε)(1+|t|)^(1/4+ε). The principal primitive character is separated before applying the quadratic fourth-moment theorem. A pole-aware strip extension is a separate lemma. Here L2 is oddLContinuation, not the totalized naive LSeries.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Match (16) with the odd squarefree discriminants and the four twists.
Keep its ε-loss and vertical-parameter dependence.
Feed partial summation with the selected bound into the d0 series.

proofDependencies.title: Pole-aware strip first moment
proofDependencies.statement: Fix a compact real interval I and ε>0. There exist C,N>0 such that for σ∈I, X≥1 and t∈R, Σd≤X,d odd |(σ+it−1)L2(σ+it,χdψi)| ≤ C X^(max(1,3/2−σ)+ε)(1+|t|)^N. At s=1 the term denotes the analytic extension of (s−1)L2(s), not totalized multiplication. Constants depend on I and ε, not X,t or i. The summands are the absolute values of the entire functions H_i,d=DoubleSeries.poleClearL.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: On compact right strips use the fourth moment, Hölder and square-factor decomposition, separating the principal ζ2 contribution.
Reflect strips left of 1/2; the conductor factor d^(1/2−σ) gives the exponent 3/2−σ. Track the gamma and pole-clearing factors as polynomial height bounds.
Uniform strip constants must be proved by the same smoothed-sum argument, not inferred from pointwise O constants.

proofDependencies.title: Locally uniform convergence in R1
proofDependencies.statement: The pole-cleared squarefree expression is holomorphic on R1={Rew>1,Res+Rew>3/2}; its only possible polar line there is s=1, from the trivial inner twist.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Use the first-moment bound for Res≥1/2.
Apply the quadratic functional equation and its conductor growth for Res<1/2.
Sum on compact strict sub-tubes and separate the trivial-character pole.

proofDependencies.title: The swap functional equation
proofDependencies.statement: The 16-vector continuation satisfies Z(s,w)=A Z(w,s) wherever defined meromorphically.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Interchange the absolutely convergent odd sums.
Expand the quadratic-reciprocity sign using the finite character table.
Use identity continuation from the nonempty overlap.

proofDependencies.title: The reflection functional equation
proofDependencies.statement: The 16-vector continuation satisfies Z(s,w)=B(s)Z(1−s,s+w−1/2) as an equality of meromorphic germs.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Separate odd squarefree d0 and residue classes.
Use the primitive real-character functional equation and the deleted factor at2.
Observe that s+2w is invariant and that 2w and 2s+2w−1 are exchanged.

proofDependencies.title: The zero block that removes a false pole
proofDependencies.statement: B(s) is holomorphic on Res<1 and its principal-twist block vanishes at s=0. This cancels the reflected principal w=1 pole where its image would otherwise introduce an extra pole; it does not assert that every block vanishes at zero.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Use the gamma quotient with parity and the Euler factor ratio.
Cancel apparent denominators at their removable zeros.
At s=0 in the first block, the reciprocal gamma zero cancels the candidate transported pole.

proofDependencies.title: Functional branches agree on overlaps
proofDependencies.statement: On every connected nonempty open overlap of the R1,αR1,βR2,αR3 tube components, both branches have the same meromorphic germ: transport to the original absolute-convergence tube and use the identity theorem after clearing all encountered pole factors. Intersections used here are convex real tubes, hence connected.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Clear the finite polar factors on each overlap. The transported functional equations agree on a nonempty absolute-convergence subdomain. The identity theorem extends agreement to the connected convex tube intersection; perform each successive gluing with that same normalization.

proofDependencies.title: Cancellation of spurious reflected poles
proofDependencies.statement: During the R2→R3 gluing, the only candidate new pole beyond s=1,w=1,s+w=3/2 is the reflected principal-twist pole through s=0. The principal block B1(0)=0 cancels it. Track pole orders as germs; multiplying totalized zero values is insufficient.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Separate the principal residue term in the reflected branch. Its scalar pole has order at most one and the entire principal reflection block vanishes at zero. Multiply as analytic germs, using the order inequality to remove the candidate pole.

proofDependencies.title: Gluing the four continued tubes
proofDependencies.statement: R2=α(R1)∪R1; R3=β(R2)∪R2; R4=α(R3)∪R3. The functional equations agree on their nonempty open overlaps and the gluing leaves possible poles only at s=1,w=1,s+w=3/2.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Check the explicit inequalities defining each tube, as on pp.363–364.
Use holomorphic uniqueness on the overlaps after multiplying by the three linear pole factors.
Use B1(0)=0 to remove the candidate s=0 hyperplane.

locators.locator: §3 proof of Lemma 2, tube R1 and its images (36), pp.363–364

proofDependencies.title: Bochner tube extension
proofDependencies.statement: For connected open Ω⊆R² and f holomorphic on TΩ, there is a unique holomorphic F on Tconv(Ω) with F=f on TΩ. The imaginary directions are unrestricted. This is a theorem on tubes, not on arbitrary punctured complex domains.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: The exact connected-tube convex-hull extension is the external Bochner input. DGH Proposition 4.6 states it without its primary proof, so the packet records proof acquisition as a gap. Uniqueness on the convex tube follows from the analytic identity theorem.

proofDependencies.title: Bound survives tube extension
proofDependencies.statement: Under the Bochner hypotheses, if M≥0 and |f(z)|≤M for all z∈TΩ, then its extension F satisfies |F(z)|≤M throughout Tconv(Ω).
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: For every |a|>M, extend 1/(f−a) to the convex tube. The holomorphic identity (F−a)G=1 follows from uniqueness.
Thus F avoids every value outside the closed radius-M disk.

proofDependencies.title: Affine dihedral action
proofDependencies.statement: The two maps α,β satisfy α²=β²=id and (αβ)^6=id. At (2,3), the six iterates of αβ are distinct, so its order is exactly six. These transformations act on the real-part tube bases as well as on C².
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Compute alpha beta as an affine map and iterate it six times symbolically. Both generators square to the identity; the six images of (2,3) are distinct and certify exact order six.

proofDependencies.title: Real shell convex hull
proofDependencies.statement: After R4=R3∪αR3, set R5=R4∪βR4 and R6=R5∪αR5. The complement of the real-part base of R6 is the closed twelve-gon Ω with successive vertices (1,1),(1/2,1),(0,3/2),(0,1),(−1/2,1),(0,1/2),(0,0),(1/2,0),(1,−1/2),(1,0),(3/2,0),(1,1/2). It lies in x²+y²≤3, so the connected annulus 4<x²+y²<5 lies in the glued base and its convex hull contains Ω. The earlier R4 alone does not have bounded complement.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Write each transported tube as explicit linear inequalities, using both remaining functional-equation transports R4→R5→R6.
Check the complement by its twelve successive boundary segments. Bound every vertex by x²+y²≤3; convexity of the disk gives the polygon bound.
The open annulus is connected and its convex hull is the disk of radius sqrt(5); use the bounded normalization on its entire imaginary tube.

proofDependencies.title: Gamma reflection block growth
proofDependencies.statement: On each closed strip a≤Res≤b<1, the filled r_i,η(s) and hence entries of B(s) are bounded by C(1+|Ims|)^N. Stirling for the Gamma quotient gives a power of height; the Euler denominator has modulus at least 1−2^(b−1)>0 when e≠0. On a bounded height interval use holomorphy and compactness.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Separate the four conductor factors, whose moduli depend only on Res.
Apply the vertical-strip Stirling ratio estimate away from bounded height; reciprocal Gamma fills the bounded-height removable points.
Use the stated uniform lower bound for the restored Euler denominator.

proofDependencies.title: Bounded normalization on the shell tube
proofDependencies.statement: On the annular shell 4<Res²+Rew²<5 used in the last continuation step, the cleared branch F=PZ has a bound C(1+|Ims|)^N(1+|Imw|)^N from the R1 estimate and transported reflection estimates. Choose an integer M≥N. Then F/[(3+s)^M(3+w)^M] is holomorphic and bounded on the shell tube, and its denominator has no zero on the full tube Res²+Rew²<5. Bochner bounded extension of this normalized function fills the hole; multiplying the denominator restores F.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Cover the closed real annulus 4≤Res²+Rew²≤5 by finitely many transported convergence regions, using germ agreement on overlaps. It lies inside their union because the excluded polygon has squared radius at most 9/4. Compactness supplies uniform constants for its open subannulus.
Retain polynomial height estimates in both variables under the finitely many affine transformations.
Since |Res|,|Rew|<√5<3, |3+s| and |3+w| are bounded below and dominate 1+|Ims| and 1+|Imw| up to a fixed positive scalar.

locators.locator: Final part of Lemma 2 proof, pp.363–364

proofDependencies.title: Filling the remaining real twelve-gon
proofDependencies.statement: Let Ω⊆R² be connected and open and let f be holomorphic on TΩ={z:Re z∈Ω}. It has a unique holomorphic extension to Tconv(Ω) (Bochner). If |f|≤M on TΩ, the extension has the same bound. Apply this to the pole-cleared branch on the annular real shell around the omitted twelve-gon.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Extend f by Bochner. For each complex a with |a|>M, also extend 1/(f−a). The identity (f−a)/(f−a)=1 extends by uniqueness, so the extended f never takes such an a.
Apply the shell hull to each cleared component; only the local shell bound enters.

proofDependencies.title: Self-dual versus integral-normalized measures
proofDependencies.statement: For the alternating binary-cubic pairing [x,y]=x1y4−x2y3/3+x3y2/3−x4y1, self-dual dx=|3|^(−1)∏dxj. If each coordinate self-dual measure gives O mass q^(−e/2), then dx(O⁴)=|3|^(−1)q^(−2e). With dg(GL2(O))=1, bF=|3|^(−1)q^(−2e)(1−q^(−1))(1−q^(−2)). Dividing by dx(O⁴) yields the integral-normalized constant; at residue characteristic 3 the |3| factor cannot be discarded before this conversion.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Compute the determinant of the alternating pairing relative to the coordinate self-dual measure. The two 1/3 entries contribute the factor |3|^(-1). Multiply four coordinate lattice masses and then the normalized GL2 integral factor, retaining the different exponent.

proofDependencies.title: Binary cubic orbital Jacobian
proofDependencies.statement: For an open orbit α and representative xα, the map g↦g·xα has covering degree oα. Its measure change satisfies dx/|P(x)|=bF dg along each sheet, with bF as in the local measure normalization. Consequently ∫αΦ dx=bF|P(xα)|/oα ∫G|det g|²Φ(g·xα)dg.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Differentiate the orbit map in four GL2 matrix coordinates and use its discriminant Jacobian.
Account for the finite stabilizer covering, then evaluate the remaining Haar scalar on the Iwasawa normalization.

proofDependencies.title: Adelic binary cubic convergence
proofDependencies.statement: For Res>1, the right-quotient binary-cubic integral converges absolutely and locally uniformly in s and is a tempered distribution in Φ. Wright uses exponent |det|^u with Reu>2; here u=2s.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Use the compact-times-Siegel-set majorant of Lemma 3.1, p.515.
Cover nonsingular rational forms by x1≠0 or x2≠0; apply the Schwartz lattice-sum bound of Lemma 1.1.
Integrate its explicit torus majorant for exponent σ>2 with decay parameter α>2nσ.

proofDependencies.title: Adelic orbital unfolding
proofDependencies.statement: For Res>1 and a Schwartz–Bruhat Φ, Z(Φ,s)=Σ[x]∈GL2(F)\V(F)^ns |Stab(x)|^(−1)∫GL2(A_F)|det g|^(2s)Φ(g·x)dg. All rearrangements are justified by absolute convergence. Integral lattice restrictions require all class-group components, as the S-integral comparison shows.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Partition nonsingular rational forms by rational GL2 orbits. Absolute convergence permits exchanging the orbit sum and quotient integral. Lift each orbit integral to GL2(A) and divide by its finite stabilizer; the lattice comparison must sum all ideal-class components.

proofDependencies.title: All class-group components in unfolding
proofDependencies.statement: The S-integral adelic zeta decomposes over the full double quotient G(A_S)\G(A)/G(F), not just the identity lattice. Each component uses its associated rank-two lattice, binary-cubic lattice and arithmetic stabilizer. This is the analytic interface needed for the ST extension to nonprincipal locally free modules.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Choose double-quotient representatives and transport the rational-orbit sum into each lattice.
Unfold each component with its own stabilizer. The missing general-ring parametrization remains an ST request.

proofDependencies.title: Split local factor
proofDependencies.statement: For DW standard Φ1 and u=ω(π), the split auxiliary integral Iα(ω,Φ1)=(1+u)^2/(1−u). Its four disjoint valuation regions have masses 1/(1−u),u²/(1−u),u/(1−u),u/(1−u).
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Divide the support of the auxiliary orbital integral into the four valuation regions of DW. Sum the two linear contributions and the constant and quadratic contributions against the geometric tail. Their numerator is (1+u)^2.

proofDependencies.title: Unramified quadratic local factor
proofDependencies.statement: The standard quadratic auxiliary integral is (1+u²)/(1−u): its two regions have t unit or valuation one, with integral basis coordinates for the unramified quadratic extension.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Use an integral basis of the unramified quadratic extension to separate the unit and valuation-one support pieces. Their norm valuations contribute 1 and u^2, with a common geometric tail 1/(1-u).

proofDependencies.title: Ramified quadratic local factor
proofDependencies.statement: The ramified quadratic auxiliary integral is (1+u)/(1−u). In an integral basis 1,θ with θ a uniformizer, the field norm valuation gives the two disjoint support regions used in the integral. This formulation does not require residue characteristic odd.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Choose the uniformizer integral basis and distinguish the two support regions by its norm valuation. Their contributions are 1 and u over the common tail. The discriminant Jacobian stays outside this calculation, so residue characteristic two is retained.

proofDependencies.title: Unramified cubic local factor
proofDependencies.statement: The unramified cubic auxiliary integral is (1+u²+u⁴)/(1−u³)=(1−u+u²)/(1−u), from three valuation regions t of orders 0,1,2. The numerator records all three regions rather than an unjustified geometric shell law.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: The integral basis splits support according to three successive uniformizer valuations. Sum the contributions 1,u^2,u^4 against the step-three tail. Multiply the two rational expressions by their denominators to prove the simplification.

proofDependencies.title: Ramified cubic local factor
proofDependencies.statement: For a ramified cubic extension with integral generator θ a uniformizer, the three support regions give (1+u+u²)/(1−u³)=1/(1−u). Norm(θ) is a uniformizer in the base field, so this valuation computation retains wild discriminant factors in the separate orbital Jacobian.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Use the cubic uniformizer integral basis; its field norm has valuation one. The three support pieces contribute 1,u,u^2 against the step-three tail, which simplifies to 1/(1-u). Keep the wild discriminant in the preceding Jacobian.

proofDependencies.title: Five local orbital Euler factors
proofDependencies.statement: For Φ0=1_(O⁴), an unramified quasicharacter ω and a DW standard representative, put u=ω(π). Then Zα(ω,Φ0)=ηα(u)/[(1−qu³)(1−u²)], with η=(1+u)²,1+u²,1+u,1−u+u²,1 for types split, unramified quadratic, ramified quadratic, unramified cubic, ramified cubic respectively. A ramified ω gives zero. Characteristic zero permits residue characteristics 2 and 3; their discriminant and self-dual-measure factors remain in the preceding normalization.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Use the shell-removal differential identity and its integral evaluation from Propositions 3.1–3.2, pp.39–41: Z(Φ0)=(1−u)/[(1−qu³)(1−u²)] I(Φ1).
Insert the five auxiliary factors, one declaration per orbit type.
Compact determinant-character integration gives zero for ramified ω.

locators.locator: Theorem 3.1, p.42; Euler-product comparison Theorem 6.1, p.68

proofDependencies.title: Absolute convergence of cubic Shintani series
proofDependencies.statement: Every ξF,α(s) and dual series converges absolutely on Res>1.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Start with the absolute adelic convergence theorem for Re s>1, rather than the coarser uniform coefficient estimate which only proves convergence for Re s>3/2.

Apply the absolutely convergent orbit unfolding and the all-ideal-class lattice comparison. Choose nonnegative local test functions whose archimedean orbit support isolates the required signature and whose local orbital factors are nonzero.

The resulting positive orbital sum is the Shintani series times finite local factors. The dual trace-divisible lattice restricts this nonnegative sum, so it has the same convergence half-plane. This is the convergence argument of DW §6 and the LOWW statement.

locators.locator: §6, Theorem 6.2 and preceding orbital/Euler-product comparison, pp.68–71

proofDependencies.title: Entire truncated cubic integral
proofDependencies.statement: Restrict the right-quotient integral to |det g|≥1. The resulting Z+(Φ,u), with exponent u, is entire and a tempered distribution in Φ. On every compact u set its derivatives are dominated by the Siegel-set Schwartz majorant; u=2s is the arithmetic convention.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: On the truncated determinant range choose a common Schwartz-decay exponent for the compact parameter set.
The convergence proof majorant absorbs log powers from u derivatives.
Parameter integration gives entireness; its seminorm bound gives continuity in Φ.

proofDependencies.title: Poisson decomposition of the global integral
proofDependencies.statement: On Reu>2, additive Poisson on F^4 gives Z(Φ,u)=Z+(Φ,u)+Z+(Fourier Φ,2−u)+I(Φ,u), where I is the integral over |det|≤1 of the Fourier-transformed singular theta sum minus the original singular theta sum, including the determinant Jacobian |det|^(−2). The singular locus has exactly zero, triple-root and double-root rational orbits.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Apply Poisson to the full lattice sum, subtract the singular terms, and split at |det|=1.
Invert g in the small-determinant integral and use the paired contragredient action.
All sums and integrals are absolutely convergent on the initial right domain.

proofDependencies.title: Rank-one smoothing extracts the quotient integral
proofDependencies.statement: For rapidly vertically decreasing entire ψ with ψ(2)≠0, smooth the rank-one GL2 Eisenstein series by integral_Rez=x0 ψ(z)E(z,g)/(w−z) dz/(2πi). For quotient-integrable F dominated by C t(g)^c with c<2, (w−2) integral F(g)ℰ(ψ,w,g)dg tends as w decreases to 2 to ρ0ψ(2) integral F(g)dg. Here E has constant term t^(z/2)+t^((2−z)/2)φ_F(z), φ_F(z)=Z_F(z−1)/Z_F(z), and ρ0=Res Z_F(1)/Z_F(2).
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: The AS rank-one specialization must supply the displayed constant term, residue and nonconstant Fourier bound of Lemma 6.3.
Shift the smoothing contour across z=2; the residue is the constant ρ0ψ(2)/(w−2).
Use its uniform weighted majorant for dominated convergence.

proofDependencies.title: Zero-orbit contribution
proofDependencies.statement: On the determinant-one quotient the smoothed singular zero contribution is I0(Φ;ψ,w)=ψ(2)Φ(0)/(w−2) for the principal character. For a nontrivial unitary character of determinant-one ideles it vanishes.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: The zero theta term is constant on the quotient. Integrate the smoothed Eisenstein constant term using its residue normalization. A nontrivial unitary determinant character integrates to zero by character orthogonality.

proofDependencies.title: Compact averaging and Fourier
proofDependencies.statement: For normalized Haar on the maximal compact U_A put MωΦ(x)=integral_U ω(det k)Φ(k·x)dk. This is again Schwartz–Bruhat, satisfies Mω²=Mω, transforms under k by ω(det k)^(−1), and Fourier(MωΦ)=M_(ω~ inverse)(Fourier Φ). Here ω~ is the unitary component of ω, not complex conjugation of an arbitrary power.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Compactness permits the parameter integral in each Schwartz seminorm.
Change k to kh in normalized Haar for equivariance and idempotence.
The determinant Jacobian is 1 on U_A; the contragredient action and Fourier change of variables give the last identity.

proofDependencies.title: Singular distributions from Tate integrals
proofDependencies.statement: T1Φ(t)=Φ(0,0,0,t), T2Φ(t)=integral_A Φ(0,0,t,u)du are Schwartz–Bruhat functions. Their Tate zeta integrals converge normally for Re z>1, continue with simple poles at 0,1, and have residues −Φ(0), integral Φ(0,0,0,u)du for T1 and −integral Φ(0,0,0,u)du, integral Φ(0,0,t,u)dtdu for T2. Apply this to MωΦ with twists ω~ inverse and ω~ to obtain Σ1(ω,Φ,z), Σ2(ω,Φ,z). The residue distributions used globally are Σ1 at z=2/3 and Σ2 at z=−1.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Partial evaluation and partial integration preserve the Schwartz class.
Use the Tate continuation/residue supplier, rather than a new one-dimensional zeta theory.
Fourier inversion on the alternating pairing supplies the two partial-transform identities of Proposition 5.2.

proofDependencies.title: Unfold the triple-root orbit
proofDependencies.statement: The nonzero triple-root locus is parametrized by cosets in GL2(F)/B(F) together with a nonzero scalar α on the line represented by (0,0,0,α). The Borel preserves that line but is not the stabilizer of each fixed nonzero vector. Summing over α makes the expression independent of the coset representatives. On the determinant-one quotient its smoothed integral unfolds to the idele/Tate expression in Σ1(ω,Φ,(z+1)/3) and Σ1(ω,Φ,(3−z)/3), with the factor 1/3 from the cubic torus map. Compact averaging and rational reindexing preserve the chosen measures.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Parametrize triple-root lines by GL2(F)/B(F) and sum all nonzero rational scalars on each line. Borel rescaling permutes this scalar sum; it does not fix each vector.
Unfold the rational orbit, telescope the F× sum against the idele quotient and substitute the cubic torus variable.
The two Eisenstein constant terms give the two displayed Tate parameters.

proofDependencies.title: Triple-root contour residues
proofDependencies.statement: Modulo a function holomorphic for Rew>1, the principal-character triple-root smoothed term is ρ0ψ(2)Σ1(Φ)/[3(w−2)] + φ_F(3)ψ(3) integral(MΦ)(0,0,0,t)dt/(w−3). The Σ1 symbol denotes the continued Tate restriction at 2/3. Vertical contour bounds are those of the Tate and rank-one smoothing inputs.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Move each Tate-parameter contour into the strip where its only crossed poles are known.
Collect the z=2 Eisenstein residue and z=3 Tate residue; retain the cubic Jacobian 1/3.

proofDependencies.title: Unfold the double-root orbit
proofDependencies.statement: The double-root orbit is represented by (0,0,α,0). After unfolding and a Schwartz lattice majorant, the nonconstant Eisenstein contribution is holomorphic for Rew>1. The remaining two contours have Tate parameters −1−z and z−3, exactly as in the last display of p.531.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Unfold the Borel orbit and its two determinant-one idele variables.
Use Lemma 6.3 with decay exponent N>1 and the Schwartz bound with A>N[F:Q] to dominate the nonconstant contribution.
Telescope the rational α sum and substitute the remaining additive coordinate.

proofDependencies.title: Double-root contour residues
proofDependencies.statement: Modulo a function holomorphic for Rew>1, the principal double-root term is ρ0ψ(2)Σ2(Φ)/(w−2) − φ_F(3)ψ(3)integral(MΦ)(0,0,0,t)dt/(w−3) + φ_F(4)ψ(4)integral(MΦ)(0,0,t,u)dtdu/(w−4). Here Σ2 is evaluated at −1; these three residues use the same normalized measures as the triple-root term.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Shift the two unfolded Tate contours and collect the poles at the displayed parameters. The first residue uses Sigma2(-1); the remaining residues are the one- and two-variable restriction integrals. Preserve the signs from opposite contour shifts and the common compact average.

proofDependencies.title: Cancel the extra smoothing poles
proofDependencies.statement: Fourier inversion makes the z=3 and z=4 residues cancel in the Fourier-minus-original singular difference. Its determinant-one quotient integral is [Fourier Φ(0)−Φ(0)]/ρ0 + [Σ1(Fourier Φ)−Σ1(Φ)]/3 + Σ2(Fourier Φ)−Σ2(Φ), for the principal character.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Combine the three singular-orbit residue expressions and use the partial Fourier-inversion identities.
Apply the smoothing residue limit; the cancelled w=3,4 terms cannot enter the global radial integral.

proofDependencies.title: Integrate the singular radial powers
proofDependencies.statement: For the principal exponent u, I(Φ,u)=−1/2{[Fourier Φ(0)/(2−u)+Φ(0)/u]/ρ0 + [Σ1(Fourier Φ)/(5/3−u)+Σ1(Φ)/(u−1/3)]/3 + Σ2(Fourier Φ)/(2−u)+Σ2(Φ)/u}, as meromorphic germs. The factor 1/2 comes from determinant scaling, and Fourier dilation has the fourth-power Jacobian.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Apply the two dilation homogeneities of Lemma 5.3 to the three summands.
Integrate the resulting real powers on (0,1); use analytic continuation for the rational expression.

proofDependencies.title: Adelic cubic continuation and equation
proofDependencies.statement: The principal adelic Z(Φ,u) continues with only simple possible poles at u=0,1/3,5/3,2 and obeys Z(Φ,u)=Z(Fourier Φ,2−u). Its residue at 2 is [Fourier Φ(0)/ρ0+Σ2(Fourier Φ)]/2 and its residue at 5/3 is Σ1(Fourier Φ)/6. These are adelic residues in variable u; conversion to s=u/2 divides residues by 2.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: The two truncated terms are entire; the rational singular expression lists the poles.
Exchange Φ and Fourier Φ and replace u by 2−u; Fourier inversion removes the sign by the rational scalar −1.
Read the two rational-term coefficients, including the variable-change Jacobian.

proofDependencies.title: Fourier transform of the integral lattice
proofDependencies.statement: For self-dual binary-cubic pairing at v, Fourier(1_(O_v^4))(x)=|3|_v^(−1)q_v^(−2e_v)·1_(O_v^4)(δ_v(x1,3x2,3x3,x4)), where δ_v generates the local different in the source convention. This identifies the trace-divisible dual selector and retains the factor at v|3.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Compute the annihilator of the coordinate integral lattice under the alternating pairing and different-normalized additive character. Fourier of its indicator is its self-dual mass times the annihilator indicator. The two middle coordinates acquire 3, yielding the trace-divisible dual.

proofDependencies.title: Archimedean Fourier comparison
proofDependencies.statement: After exponent u=2s, the real orbital Fourier matrix is the common factor 3^(6s−3)π^(−4s)Γ(s)^2Γ(s−1/6)Γ(s+1/6) times the real sine matrix; its real off-diagonal split-to-nonsplit entry carries the factor 3. The complex scalar is the squared gamma normalization times the four-sine factor. Transport these self-dual local equations to the integral-normalized arithmetic series before collecting the global D and 3 factors.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: The real matrix is Theorem 4.1, whose original Shintani distribution proof remains the exact local-Fourier gap.
The complex proof uses the Gaussian polynomial-differential recurrence, a period-two entire quotient and its finite Fourier support; Theorem 4.2 fixes the scalar.
Use reflection and multiplication formulas to express the arithmetic-normalized sine factors.

locators.locator: DW Theorems 4.1–4.2, pp.48–51; LOWW (3.1) and Proposition 3.7(3), pp.12–13

proofDependencies.title: Cubic meromorphic continuation
proofDependencies.statement: Each ordinary ξF,α extends meromorphically to C with at most simple poles at 1 and 5/6. Its continuation agrees with the order-weighted series on Res>1.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Unfold the adelic continuation into all ideal-class components, apply the five local factors and finite dual-lattice Fourier comparison, and compare archimedean orbital integrals. Cancel the extraneous adelic factors, leaving the two arithmetic simple poles.

proofDependencies.title: Order-one bound for cubic clearance
proofDependencies.statement: For each signature α and ε>0 there is Cε>0 such that the entire cleared cubic function satisfies |CF,α(s)|≤exp(Cε(1+|s|)^(1+ε)) for all s∈C. This is order at most one, independent of the algebraic pole-clearance construction.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: The cited theorem states order one for the exponent-u series; replacing u by 2s preserves that order.

A quantitative proof requires the vertical estimates for the truncated adelic distribution and archimedean factors; this exact source-proof input is a recorded gap, not a consequence of merely removing two poles.

proofDependencies.title: Archimedean coefficients vanish to degree order
proofDependencies.statement: Every cαβ(s) vanishes to order at least n=r1+2r2 at s=1; each real factor has order≥1 and each complex factor has order2.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Expand sin(πs) and sin(2πs) at1.
At a complex place only the squared sine vanishes; the shifted sine factors are nonzero.
Add orders under the finite product.

locators.locator: §3.2 equation (3.1), p.12, and proof of Lemma 3.8, p.13

proofDependencies.title: The global prefactor is a unit at one
proofDependencies.statement: The gamma/discriminant prefactor in the cubic functional equation is holomorphic and nonzero at s=1, since its gamma arguments are1,5/6 and7/6.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Check all three gamma arguments are positive at1.
Use gamma holomorphy and nonvanishing there.
Use positive-base exponential powers for the discriminant and3/π factors.

locators.locator: §3.2 Proposition 3.7(3), p.12, and proof of Lemma 3.8, p.13

proofDependencies.title: Simple poles of the dual cubic Shintani series
proofDependencies.statement: For each number field F and archimedean signature α, the dual ξhatF,α has a meromorphic continuation with no poles except possible simple poles at 1 and 5/6. In particular (s−1)ξhatF,α(s) is holomorphic near 1.
hypotheses: Use the trace-divisible dual series of cubic-shintani-series, with the LOWW normalizations.
proofSketch: Use the original DW Theorem 6.2 decomposition with the trace-divisible finite test function identified by local-finite-fourier-dual.
The same truncated-entire and singular-residue argument bounds pole orders by one; coefficient positivity alone does not imply this.

proofDependencies.title: The weighted cubic-coefficient bound
proofDependencies.statement: For every ε>0 and real σ>3/2, ξF,α(σ)≪[F:Q],σ,ε D^(1/2+ε)h2(F). Prove the separate split/quadratic-factor and cubic-field contributions using LOWW Lemma3.5 and the orders formula; the field-count input remains with ST.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Decompose cubic étale algebras into split, quadratic-factor and cubic-field types.
Use the appropriate discriminant/count bound for each.
Sum the order-index factor with σ>3/2 and retain h2(F).

proofDependencies.title: Reflected vertical bound from the matrix equation
proofDependencies.statement: For σ<−1/2 and |t|≥1, the functional equation gives ξF,α(σ+it)≪ε,n,σ h2(F)D^(5/2−4σ+ε)(1+|t|)^(n(2−4σ)+ε), using the right-half-plane dual bound. Constants depend on the fixed real strip.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Bound the dual by the ordinary positive-coefficient series at1−σ>3/2.
Apply Stirling to the gamma factors and combine with sine growth.
Multiply the functional-equation factor D^(2−4σ) by the right-half-plane bound h2(F)D^(1/2+ε). The combined exponent is 5/2−4σ+ε; retain the stated height power.

locators.locator: §3.2 proof of Lemma 3.11, left-boundary estimate, p.14; combine Proposition 3.7(3) with Lemma 3.10

proofDependencies.title: The compact discrete-spectrum input
proofDependencies.statement: AS.4 supplies a complete orthonormal scalar eigenbasis with finite multiplicities and Weyl counting N(Λ)~area(X)Λ/(4π). Connectedness gives the simple zero eigenvalue.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Specialize the compact Hilbert-sum decomposition.
Identify the scalar positive Laplacian and its kernel.
Use the supplied heat/Weyl asymptotics rather than treating compactness alone as a spectrum theorem.

proofDependencies.title: Weyl bounds imply spectral summability
proofDependencies.statement: For a nonnegative spectrum with one zero mode, finite multiplicities and counting function N(R)≤CR for R≥1, Σλj>0 λj^(−σ) converges for σ>1, locally uniformly in complex σ on Res>1. Also Σexp(−tλj) converges locally uniformly for t>0 and Σλj>0 λj^(−2)<∞.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Use dyadic blocks 2^k≤λ<2^(k+1), each of size O(2^k).
For complex parameters take the real-part infimum on the compact domain.
Exponential decay dominates the same dyadic counts for heat sums.

proofDependencies.title: Heat Mellin identity
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Use positive-spectrum Weyl bounds to dominate the small-t integral.
Use the positive spectral gap for exponential decay as t→∞.
Apply dominated interchange and the scalar gamma integral term by term.

proofDependencies.title: Exponential heat decay after zero subtraction
proofDependencies.statement: If λ1>0 and the Weyl bound holds, then for t≥1, |H(t)−1|≤C exp(−λ1 t/2), with C=Σj≥1 exp(−λj/2)<∞. Consequently the Mellin integral from 1 to infinity is entire in its parameter.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Monotonicity gives lambda_j>=lambda_1 for all positive modes. Split exp(-t lambda_j) into exp(-t lambda_j/2) times itself and bound one factor by exp(-t lambda_1/2). Weyl summability bounds the remaining sum at t>=1; every Mellin derivative is integrable against this exponential tail.

proofDependencies.title: Subtracting small-time heat coefficients
proofDependencies.statement: Write H(t)=Σj≥0 exp(−tλj), including its simple zero mode. The positive spectral Mellin integral uses H(t)−1. If H(t)=Σk=0..N ak t^(k−1)+O(t^N), then subtract Σk=0..N ak t^(k−1)−1. Its integral on (0,1) is Σk=0..N ak/(s+k−1)−1/s. The remainder integral is holomorphic for Re s>−N under locally uniform remainder bounds; thus the coefficient at s=0 is a1−1, not a1.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Obtain uniform heat-remainder bounds from the heat-kernel supplier.
Split the Mellin integral of H(t)−1 at 1; subtract the zero mode along with the finite heat expansion.
Integrate the polynomial to Σ ak/(s+k−1)−1/s and dominate the remainder locally for Re s>−N.

proofDependencies.title: Holomorphic remainder after heat subtraction
proofDependencies.statement: If H(t)=Σk=0..N ak t^(k−1)+RN(t), with |RN(t)|≤CN t^N on (0,1], then integral_0^1 t^(z−1)RN(t)dt is holomorphic for Rez>−N, locally uniformly in z. For the positive heat trace H−1 the rational terms are Σk=0..N ak/(z+k−1)−1/z.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: On a compact parameter set use the lower real-part bound −N+δ and integrable majorant t^(δ−1).
Parameter derivatives introduce powers of log t, still integrable; the rational terms are separate germ identities.

locators.locator: §4 (4.5)–(4.6), pp.14–15; positive-spectrum correction from Sarnak (1.3), p.603

proofDependencies.title: Compact geodesic-series majorant
proofDependencies.statement: The primitive length spectrum has positive systole ℓ0, finite counts below any height and Nprim(T)≤Cexp(T). These imply compact-normal convergence of Σp,m≥1 exp(−msℓp)/(m(1−exp(−mℓp))) on Res>1, including its s derivatives. Each primitive conjugacy class uses exactly the orientation convention of the Gaussian trace supplier.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Use the positive systole to bound the geometric denominator away from zero. Sum in unit length intervals using the exponential count; on a compact right half-plane the surplus real exponent absorbs the polynomial factors produced by derivatives.

proofDependencies.title: Logarithmic derivative of the primitive product
proofDependencies.statement: For Res>1, expand log(1−e^(−(s+k)ℓp)) and sum k geometrically. This gives Z′/Z=Σp,m≥1 ℓp e^(−msℓp)/(1−e^(−mℓp)), locally uniformly.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Use the geodesic-count bound with a strict real-part margin.
Justify derivative and summation interchanges.
Sum the k-series and preserve the primitive/power weights.

proofDependencies.title: The compact scalar heat trace input
proofDependencies.statement: For t>0, H(t)=area(X)/(4π)∫R r tanh(πr)e^(−t(r²+1/4))dr +Σp,m≥1 ℓp/[2sinh(mℓp/2)] · e^(−t/4−(mℓp)²/(4t))/√(4πt). Class multiplicities agree with the primitive list fixed above. There are no cusp, elliptic or continuous-spectrum terms in this selected compact torsion-free case.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Supply the heat test function and its Fourier transform with exact constants.
Prove the trace formula accepts this noncompactly supported test function by approximation and convergence.
Match spectral, identity and primitive hyperbolic terms.

locators.locator: §5 equations (5.1)–(5.3), p.16, scalar trivial twist m=0; remove the 1/4 operator shift; no elliptic terms

proofDependencies.title: Elementary half-order Laplace integral
proofDependencies.statement: For a>0 and Rew>0, integral_0^infinity t^(−3/2) exp(−w²t−a²/(4t))dt=(2sqrtπ/a)exp(−aw), initially on Re(w²)>0 and then by holomorphic continuation in Rew>0. The elementary z=0 half-order evaluation avoids a general Bessel-function package.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: For positive real w reduce by t=a²/(4v²) to a Gaussian integral and differentiate the usual Gaussian parameter identity.
Use a common integrable majorant on compact subsets of Re(w²)>0, Rew>0.
The resulting exponential expression extends to the right w half-plane.

proofDependencies.title: Normal convergence of the hyperbolic transform
proofDependencies.statement: For the scalar compact trace, choose Rew>0 and Re(w²)>C with w=s−1/2 and C large enough for the geodesic count. The heat transform is jointly holomorphic in z,s on this region, locally uniform for every compact z set; sum, integral and z derivative may be interchanged. Continuation, not the integral itself, is then used outside this region.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Use the exponential length bound and the systole to dominate each term uniformly for compact parameter sets.
Integrable decay at 0 comes from exp(−ℓ²/(4t)); at infinity it comes from Re(w²)>C.
Log powers from z derivatives retain the same exponential majorant.

locators.locator: §5 Lemmas 5.1–5.3, pp.16–18, with the explicit safe region

proofDependencies.title: Hyperbolic transform is the Selberg logarithm
proofDependencies.statement: For real s>1, the Laplace–Mellin transform of the hyperbolic heat contribution in the shifted determinant has derivative at Mellin exponent0 equal to−log ZΓ(s). This is the scalar specialization of JSS Proposition5.4; the integral proof uses the explicit Laplace identity and the compact-uniform geodesic majorant.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Use e^(−t(s−1/2)²) after factoring e^(−t/4) from the heat trace.
Evaluate the scalar Gaussian Laplace–Mellin integral term by term.
Use the absolute geodesic sum and the primitive product expansion.

locators.locator: §5 Lemmas 5.1–5.3 and Proposition 5.4, pp.17–18; determinant proof §6

proofDependencies.title: Identity contribution and Barnes normalization
proofDependencies.statement: Let C=area(X)/(4π)=g−1. The scalar identity factor is I_g(s)=exp(2C[s log(2π)+s(1−s)+logΓ(s)−2logG(s+1)]), where G is the classical Barnes G-function normalized by G(1)=1, G(s+1)=Γ(s)G(s) and the source asymptotic expansion. The full normalization/asymptotic input is required; recurrence alone is insufficient.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Differentiate the identity Laplace–Mellin term in s and evaluate the contour integral as the digamma combination in JSS(6.5).
Use the normalized Barnes logarithmic derivative (source(2.8)).
Recover the integration constant from the large-real-s asymptotics, as in the final paragraph of the proof.

Check the scalar derivative −2C(2s−1)ψ(s) using (2.8). This agrees with the identity heat transform and (8.4). Do not specialize the incompatible Gamma coefficient in (6.2); source issue E48 records that discrepancy.

locators.locator: §6 proof of Theorem 6.1, (6.5)–(6.7) and asymptotic constant, pp.21–24; (2.8)–(2.9), p.9; scalar (8.4), p.27

proofDependencies.title: Two-parameter shifted spectral zeta
proofDependencies.statement: On Reu>0, Rez>1 define ζu(z)=Σj≥0 exp(−z Log(λj+u)) with the principal logarithm. Compact-uniform Weyl bounds give joint holomorphy. Heat subtraction with exp(−ut) continues it meromorphically in z, jointly holomorphic in u, and regular at z=0. It satisfies ∂u ζu(z)=−z ζu(z+1) where both sides are initially convergent, hence as germs.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Bound lambda+u away from the principal logarithm cut on compact subsets of Re u>0. Weyl estimates dominate the series and derivatives for Re z>1. Multiply the full heat expansion by exp(-ut), subtract finitely many terms, and continue the resulting Mellin germs jointly.

locators.locator: §4 Laplace–Mellin continuation, pp.13–15; Theorem 6.1 determinant argument, p.20

proofDependencies.title: Genus-one determinant product
proofDependencies.statement: Let ζ+ be the positive spectral continuation and F(z) its analytic pole clearance (z−1)ζ+(z) near 1. The shifted determinant extends as D(u)=u exp(−ζ+′(0)+F′(1)u)∏j≥1(1+u/λj)exp(−u/λj). The product is normally convergent on all compact u sets since Σλj^(−2)<∞. On Reu>0 it equals exp(−∂z ζu(0)).
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Differentiate log(D(u)/u) twice; heat/Mellin differentiation gives −Σj≥1(λj+u)^(−2).
The genus-one product has the same second derivative, so the quotient is exp(a+bu).
At u=0 the constant is det′Δ; the linear coefficient is the finite part of ζ+ at 1, namely F′(1).

proofDependencies.title: Branch-independent identity factor
proofDependencies.statement: For integer g≥2, the scalar identity factor has the single-valued meromorphic form I_g(s)=(2π)^(2(g−1)s) exp(2(g−1)s(1−s)) Γ(s)^(2(g−1))/G(s+1)^(4(g−1)). It equals the stated exponential logarithmic formula on a simply connected right-half-plane. Its integer exponents remove logarithm branch ambiguity.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Exponentiate the logarithmic formula on a simply connected right-half-plane. The integer genus-dependent exponents turn the Gamma and Barnes factors into a single-valued meromorphic function. Equality on the original domain identifies its continuation.

locators.locator: Scalar formula (8.4), p.27, checked against §6 (6.5)–(6.7), pp.21–23; the conflicting literal specialization of (6.2), p.20, is recorded in E48

proofDependencies.title: Exact shifted determinant zero divisor
proofDependencies.statement: D(u) vanishes exactly at u=−λj, with order equal to the eigenvalue multiplicity. Around each such u0, D(u)=(u−u0)^m h(u), with h holomorphic and nonzero at u0. The finite factors for that eigenvalue are separated from the normally convergent nonvanishing residual product.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Separate the finitely many factors for the selected eigenvalue. The other canonical factors converge normally and are nonzero locally, as is the exponential prefactor. Their product is the analytic unit multiplying the required finite power.

proofDependencies.title: Spectral quadratic pullback multiplicity
proofDependencies.statement: For q(s)=s(s−1), if D has order m at u0=−λ and q(s0)=u0, then D∘q has order m when s0≠1/2 and order 2m when s0=1/2 (necessarily λ=1/4). This uses q(s)−q(s0)=(s−s0)(s+s0−1); at s0=1/2 it is (s−1/2)².
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Factor q(s)-q(s0)=(s-s0)(s+s0-1). The second factor is a unit unless s0=1/2; at that point both factors coincide. Substitute into the local determinant factorization to obtain orders m and 2m.

locators.locator: Zagier §1 spectral relation, p.2; polynomial pullback refinement

proofDependencies.title: Identity factor at spectral points
proofDependencies.statement: I_g is holomorphic and nonzero on Res>0. At s=0 it has a pole of order 2g−2, because Γ has a simple pole there and G(1)=1; at s=1 it is finite and nonzero. Thus spectral points in 0<Res<1 are unaffected, while ZΓ has order 2g−1 at 0 and order 1 at 1.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Apply the Gamma and normalized Barnes zero/pole divisors in the open right half-plane. At zero Gamma has pole one while G(s+1) is a unit, giving pole order 2g-2. Combine with the simple determinant zero at q(0)=q(1)=0.

locators.locator: §2.5 Barnes zeros, p.9; §8.1, pp.26–27; scalar identity factor

proofDependencies.title: Prime pairs with prescribed ratio and divergent weights
proofDependencies.statement: For0<β≤1, λ>1 and ε>0 there are disjoint prime pairs(pn,qn) with |(qn/pn)^β−λ|<ε and Σn qn^(−β)=∞.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Choose multiplicative intervals(λ^(2m)x0,(1+δ)λ^(2m)x0] and their alternating partners, adjustingλ toλ^(1/β).
Use the prime number theorem to inject the smaller prime list into the partner list.
The interval cardinalities divided by the upper endpoint give a divergent harmonic-m sum; β≤1 retains divergence.

proofDependencies.title: Valuation-tail cylinder ratios
proofDependencies.statement: For distinct primes p,q, the valuation swap (vp,vq)=(0,1)→(1,0) has target/source cylinder mass ratio (q/p)^β. Under the pushforward-at-target convention, the derivative of this forward map x↦(p/q)x is (p/q)^β; the inverse map has derivative (q/p)^β. Both values enter the ratio-set subgroup. The factors (1−p^(−β))(1−q^(−β)) cancel.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Multiply the two local probabilities.
Cancel the two(1−p^(−β)) normalizers in the ratio.
Use q^(−β)(1−p^(−β))(1−q^(−β)) and the prime-pair divergence.

proofDependencies.title: Prime pairs with controlled unit residues
proofDependencies.statement: For N≥1, λ>1 and ε>0, fixed-progression PNT supplies disjoint prime pairs p_n,q_n≡1(modN) with q_n/p_n→λ and Σp_n^(−1)=∞. Select primes in two disjoint proportional intervals inside successive geometric blocks, matching their counts with a fixed positive density. For 0<β≤1 the pair-swap source masses also have divergent sum.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Apply PNT in the residue class 1 mod N to paired intervals [X,(1+δ)X] and [λX,λ(1+δ)X].
Choose δ small enough for the desired ratio tolerance; matching counts are bounded below by cX/logX.
Separate successive blocks geometrically; each block contributes ≥c/logX to Σ1/p, so the block sum diverges. A diagonal tolerance choice preserves this divergence.

locators.locator: Lemma 2.3 and proof, p.5, with fixed-progression refinement

proofDependencies.title: Independent tail swaps give essential ratios
proofDependencies.statement: On a product of countable probability spaces, suppose mutually disjoint finite coordinate blocks have bijective swaps with cylinder mass ratios approaching λ>0 uniformly and a divergent sum of source cylinder masses. Then λ belongs to the ratio set of the finite-tail equivalence relation. The pushforward derivative of the inverse swap at its target equals the forward cylinder mass ratio.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Independent blocks and the divergent sum give arbitrarily distant successful swaps of positive total mass.
Approximate any positive-measure set by a finite cylinder in relative measure, then select a tail block for which source and image both meet that set with positive mass.
Apply the inverse swap so its target derivative has the stated mass ratio.

locators.locator: §1 asymptotic ratio definition and inclusion, p.2

proofDependencies.title: Ratio witnesses lift through unit cylinders
proofDependencies.statement: For any finite cylinder of integral adeles, choose its congruence level N and all its specified valuation primes. Tail pairs p,q≡1(modN), beyond those primes, act trivially on the cylinder unit residues. Their swaps therefore retain the independent-tail essential-ratio witnesses on the full adele space, rather than only on its quotient by W.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: Approximate a positive-measure set by a finite valuation-and-residue cylinder. Select tail prime pairs outside those coordinates and congruent to one at its finite level. Their rational swaps preserve specified unit residues, so independent-tail witnesses lift with positive measure.

locators.locator: Theorem 2.1 proof, pp.4–5; specialized congruence-cylinder lifting

proofDependencies.title: All positive numbers belong to the ratio set
proofDependencies.statement: For 0<β≤1 the nonsingular Q+× action on (A_f,μβ) has RatioSet=[0,∞). Its pushforward density is ρq(x)=q^β. Prime pairs with fixed unit congruences give every λ>1 after the β power; inverses give λ∈(0,1), and closure gives 0.
hypotheses: The carrier, domain and normalization hypotheses in the statement are part of the result.
proofSketch: Approximate any finite positive-measure set by a finite valuation and unit cylinder.
Use congruence-controlled disjoint pairs and the independent-tail inclusion; the inverse swap fixes the derivative convention.
Close the resulting multiplicative subgroup and use a rational-dilate exhaustion for arbitrary positive-measure sets.

proofDependencies.title: Ergodicity makes the group-measure algebra a factor
proofDependencies.statement: For the canonical μβ, the Q+× action is essentially free: qx=x with q≠1 forces x=0, a null point. For a countable essentially free nonsingular action on a standard sigma-finite measure space, the center of L∞(X,μ)⋊G equals L∞(X,μ)^G; ergodicity therefore makes it a factor.
hypotheses: The hypotheses in the statement.
proofSketch: For a nonidentity rational q, invert q-1 in the finite adeles to show its only fixed point is zero; scaling gives that point measure zero. Import the group-measure-space center theorem from OP2-factor, then use the canonical ergodicity result.

proofDependencies.title: Full positive ratio set determines type III1
